questions.q: $0.05 \mathrm{~mol}$ of an organic compound having a molar mass of $150 \mathrm{~g \, mol}^{-1}$ and containing $40 \%$ carbon by mass is subjected to complete combustion. The mass of $\mathrm{CO}_2$ produced is _____ $\mathrm{g}$.
questions.question: $0.05 \mathrm{~mol}$ of an organic compound having a molar mass of $150 \mathrm{~g \, mol}^{-1}$ and containing $40 \%$ carbon by mass is subjected to complete combustion. The mass of $\mathrm{CO}_2$ produced is _____ $\mathrm{g}$.
questions.solution:
Total mass of the organic compound taken for combustion:
$W = \text{moles} \times \text{molar mass} = 0.05 \times 150 = 7.5 \mathrm{~g}$

Mass of carbon present in this sample:
$W_{\mathrm{C}} = 40 \% \text{ of } 7.5 \mathrm{~g} = \dfrac{40}{100} \times 7.5 = 3.0 \mathrm{~g}$

Moles of carbon in the sample:
$n_{\mathrm{C}} = \dfrac{3.0}{12} = 0.25 \mathrm{~mol}$

Applying the Principle of Atomic Conservation (POAC) for carbon, all the carbon in the compound is converted to $\mathrm{CO}_2$.
Moles of $\mathrm{CO}_2$ produced = Moles of $\mathrm{C} = 0.25 \mathrm{~mol}$

Mass of $\mathrm{CO}_2$ produced:
$W_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = n_{\mathrm{CO}_2} \times \text{Molar mass of } \mathrm{CO}_2 = 0.25 \times 44 = 11 \mathrm{~g}$

Answer: $11$

questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation is:
$2\text{SO}_{2}(\text{g}) + \text{O}_{2}(\text{g}) \rightarrow 2\text{SO}_{3}(\text{g})$

Molar mass of $\text{SO}_{2} = 64\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Molar mass of $\text{O}_{2} = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Number of moles of $\text{SO}_{2} = \dfrac{12.8}{64} = 0.2\text{ mol}$
Number of moles of $\text{O}_{2} = \dfrac{4.8}{32} = 0.15\text{ mol}$

To identify the limiting reagent, divide the moles by their respective stoichiometric coefficients:
For $\text{SO}_{2}: \dfrac{0.2}{2} = 0.1$
For $\text{O}_{2}: \dfrac{0.15}{1} = 0.15$

Since $0.1 < 0.15$, $\text{SO}_{2}$ is the limiting reagent.

From the stoichiometry, $2\text{ moles}$ of $\text{SO}_{2}$ produce $2\text{ moles}$ of $\text{SO}_{3}$.
Theoretical moles of $\text{SO}_{3} = 0.2\text{ mol}$
Theoretical mass of $\text{SO}_{3} = 0.2 \times 80 = 16\text{ g}$

Given the percentage yield is $75\%$, the actual mass of $\text{SO}_{3}$ produced is:
Actual mass $= 16 \times \dfrac{75}{100} = 12\text{ g}$

Answer: $12\text{ g}$

questions.question:
A gaseous oxide of nitrogen contains $30.4\%$ of nitrogen by mass. If the vapour density of the gas is $46$, the total number of atoms present in one molecule of the gas is:

(Given: Atomic masses of $\text{N} = 14 \text{ amu}$ and $\text{O} = 16 \text{ amu}$)
questions.solution:
Mass percentage of nitrogen ($\text{N}$) $= 30.4\%$
Mass percentage of oxygen ($\text{O}$) $= 100\% - 30.4\% = 69.6\%$

Moles of $\text{N} = \dfrac{30.4}{14} \approx 2.17$
Moles of $\text{O} = \dfrac{69.6}{16} = 4.35$

Simplest molar ratio of $\text{N}$ to $\text{O}$:
$\text{N} : \text{O} = \dfrac{2.17}{2.17} : \dfrac{4.35}{2.17} = 1 : 2$

The empirical formula of the gas is $\text{NO}_2$.
Empirical formula mass $= 14 + (2 \times 16) = 46 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Molar mass of the gas $= 2 \times \text{Vapour density} = 2 \times 46 = 92 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Multiplying factor $n = \dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}} = \dfrac{92}{46} = 2$

Molecular formula $= (\text{NO}_2)_2 = \text{N}_2\text{O}_4$

Total number of atoms in one molecule of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 = 2 + 4 = 6$.

Answer: $6$

[Given: Molar atomic mass in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $Ca = 40$, $C = 12$, $O = 16$, $H = 1$, $Cl = 35.5$]
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation is:
$CaCO_3(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow CaCl_2(aq) + CO_2(g) + H_2O(l)$

Mass of pure $CaCO_3$ in the sample $= 50.0 \times \dfrac{80}{100} = 40.0\text{ g}$.
Molar mass of $CaCO_3 = 100\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
Moles of $CaCO_3 = \dfrac{40.0}{100} = 0.4\text{ mol}$.

Moles of $HCl$ available $= \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume (in L)} = 2.0 \times 0.450 = 0.9\text{ mol}$.

From the stoichiometry, $1\text{ mol}$ of $CaCO_3$ requires $2\text{ mol}$ of $HCl$.
Moles of $HCl$ required to react completely with $0.4\text{ mol}$ of $CaCO_3 = 0.4 \times 2 = 0.8\text{ mol}$.

Since the available $HCl$ ($0.9\text{ mol}$) is greater than the required $HCl$ ($0.8\text{ mol}$), $CaCO_3$ is the limiting reagent and $HCl$ is the excess reactant.

Moles of unreacted $HCl = 0.9 - 0.8 = 0.1\text{ mol}$.
Molar mass of $HCl = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
Mass of unreacted $HCl = 0.1 \times 36.5 = 3.65\text{ g}$.

Answer: $3.65\text{ g}$

(Given: Molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $\text{Mn} = 55$, $\text{O} = 16$, $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{Cl} = 35.5$. Molar volume of gas at STP $= 22.7\text{ L}$)
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the reaction is:
$\text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MnCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Cl}_2$

First, calculate the number of moles of each reactant.
Molar mass of $\text{MnO}_2 = 55 + (2 \times 16) = 87\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Moles of $\text{MnO}_2 = \dfrac{261}{87} = 3\text{ mol}$

Molar mass of $\text{HCl} = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Moles of $\text{HCl} = \dfrac{292}{36.5} = 8\text{ mol}$

From the balanced equation, $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{MnO}_2$ requires $4\text{ mol}$ of $\text{HCl}$.
So, $3\text{ mol}$ of $\text{MnO}_2$ would require $12\text{ mol}$ of $\text{HCl}$.
Since only $8\text{ mol}$ of $\text{HCl}$ is available, $\text{HCl}$ is the limiting reagent.

The amount of $\text{Cl}_2$ produced depends on the limiting reagent ($\text{HCl}$).
From the equation, $4\text{ mol}$ of $\text{HCl}$ produces $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Cl}_2$.
Moles of $\text{Cl}_2$ produced $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 8 = 2\text{ mol}$

Volume of $\text{Cl}_2$ at STP $= \text{Moles} \times \text{Molar volume}$
Volume $= 2 \times 22.7 = 45.4\text{ L}$

We are given that the volume is $x \times 10^{-1}\text{ L}$.
Therefore, $45.4 = x \times 10^{-1} \implies x = 454$.

Answer: $454$

$CaCO_3(s) \rightarrow CaO(s) + CO_2(g)$
$MgCO_3(s) \rightarrow MgO(s) + CO_2(g)$

Mass of $CO_2 = 1.84 - 0.96 = 0.88$ g
Moles of $CO_2 = \dfrac{0.88}{44} = 0.02$ mol

$x + y = 0.02$ ... (iii)

$100x + 84(0.02 - x) = 1.84$
$100x + 1.68 - 84x = 1.84$
$16x = 0.16 \Rightarrow x = 0.01$ mol

Mass of $CaCO_3 = 0.01 \times 100 = 1.00$ g.

questions.solution:
The hydrolysis of $\text{PCl}_5$ proceeds as follows:
$\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 5\text{HCl}$

Let the number of moles of pure $\text{PCl}_5$ be $n$.
Moles of $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ formed $= n$
Moles of $\text{HCl}$ formed $= 5n$

$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ is a tribasic acid, furnishing $3\text{H}^+$ ions.
$\text{HCl}$ is a monobasic acid, furnishing $1\text{H}^+$ ion.
Total moles of $\text{H}^+$ furnished $= 3n + 5n = 8n$

Moles of $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ used $= \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume (in L)} = 0.5 \times 0.2 = 0.1\text{ mol}$
Since $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ furnishes $2\text{OH}^-$ ions per formula unit, moles of $\text{OH}^- = 0.1 \times 2 = 0.2\text{ mol}$

For complete neutralization:
Moles of $\text{H}^+ =$ Moles of $\text{OH}^-$
$8n = 0.2 \Rightarrow n = 0.025\text{ mol}$

Mass of pure $\text{PCl}_5 = 0.025 \times 208.5 = 5.2125\text{ g}$

Percentage purity $= \left( \dfrac{5.2125}{10.425} \right) \times 100 = 50\%$

Answer: $50$

questions.question:

questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide is:
$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{CO} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe} + 3\text{CO}_2$

Calculate the initial number of moles of each reactant:
Molar mass of $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 = (2 \times 56) + (3 \times 16) = 112 + 48 = 160 \text{ g/mol}$
Moles of $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 = \dfrac{80}{160} = 0.5 \text{ mol}$

Molar mass of $\text{CO} = 12 + 16 = 28 \text{ g/mol}$
Moles of $\text{CO} = \dfrac{84}{28} = 3 \text{ mol}$

Identify the limiting reagent:
For $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3: \dfrac{0.5}{1} = 0.5$
For $\text{CO}: \dfrac{3}{3} = 1$

Since $0.5 < 1$, $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$ is the limiting reagent.

From the balanced equation, $1 \text{ mole}$ of $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$ produces $2 \text{ moles}$ of $\text{Fe}$.
Theoretical moles of $\text{Fe} = 2 \times 0.5 = 1 \text{ mol}$

Calculate the theoretical mass of $\text{Fe}$:
Theoretical mass = $1 \text{ mol} \times 56 \text{ g/mol} = 56 \text{ g}$

Apply the percentage yield to find the actual mass:
Actual mass = Theoretical mass $\times \dfrac{\text{Percentage yield}}{100}$
Actual mass = $56 \times 0.75 = 42 \text{ g}$

Answer: $42$

The mass ratio of C : H : O is given as $6 : 1 : 8$.

The simplest whole-number ratio of moles is:

Thus, the empirical formula of the compound is $\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{O}$.
Empirical formula mass = $12 + 2(1) + 16 = 30$

The molar mass of the compound is related to its vapor density by:
Molar mass = $2 \times \text{Vapor density} = 2 \times 45 = 90 \text{ g/mol}$

The integer multiplier $n$ is:
$n = \dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}} = \dfrac{90}{30} = 3$

The molecular formula is obtained by multiplying the empirical formula by $n$:
Molecular formula = $(\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{3} = \mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{H}_{6}\mathrm{O}_{3}$

Answer: $\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{H}_{6}\mathrm{O}_{3}$

The balanced chemical equation for the Haber process is:

Since $4 < 5$, $\text{H}_2$ is the limiting reagent.

Theoretical mass of $\text{NH}_3 = 8 \times 17.0 = 136\text{ g}$

Given that the percentage yield is $75\%$, the actual mass of ammonia produced is:
Actual mass $= 136 \times \dfrac{75}{100} = 136 \times 0.75 = 102\text{ g}$

(Given: Molar mass of Na, H, C and O are $23$, $1$, $12$ and $16$ g mol$^{-1}$ respectively)
questions.solution:
The thermal decomposition of sodium bicarbonate is given by:

$2NaHCO_3(s) \rightarrow Na_2CO_3(s) + H_2O(g) + CO_2(g)$

Molar mass of $NaHCO_3 = 23 + 1 + 12 + 3 \times 16 = 84$ g mol$^{-1}$

From the balanced equation, heating $2$ moles of $NaHCO_3$ ($2 \times 84 = 168$ g) results in the loss of $1$ mole of $H_2O$ and $1$ mole of $CO_2$ as gases.

Total mass loss for $2$ moles of $NaHCO_3 = 18$ g ($H_2O$) $+ 44$ g ($CO_2$) $= 62$ g.

Let the initial mass of the sample be $m$.

Since $62$ g of mass is lost from $168$ g of $NaHCO_3$, a mass loss of $3.1$ g corresponds to:

$m = \dfrac{168}{62} \times 3.1 = 8.4$ g.

Answer: $8.4$ g

questions.q: If $4$ moles of $\text{N}_2$ gas is mixed with $9$ moles of $\text{H}_2$ gas to synthesize ammonia, the maximum number of moles of $\text{NH}_3$ formed is _________.
questions.question: If $4$ moles of $\text{N}_2$ gas is mixed with $9$ moles of $\text{H}_2$ gas to synthesize ammonia, the maximum number of moles of $\text{NH}_3$ formed is _________.
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the synthesis of ammonia is:

$\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3$

Given:
Moles of $\text{N}_2 = 4$
Moles of $\text{H}_2 = 9$

To find the limiting reagent, divide the given moles by their respective stoichiometric coefficients:
For $\text{N}_2$: $\dfrac{4}{1} = 4$
For $\text{H}_2$: $\dfrac{9}{3} = 3$

Since $3 < 4$, $\text{H}_2$ is the limiting reagent.

From the balanced equation, $3$ moles of $\text{H}_2$ produce $2$ moles of $\text{NH}_3$.
Therefore, $9$ moles of $\text{H}_2$ will produce $\dfrac{2}{3} \times 9 = 6$ moles of $\text{NH}_3$.

The maximum number of moles of $\text{NH}_3$ formed is $6$.

Answer: $6$

Moles of $\text{MnO}_2$ left unreacted $= 2 - 1 = 1\text{ mole}$

questions.solution:
Let the mass of Hydrogen in the compound be $x$.
Then, the mass of Carbon is $9x$.
The mass of Oxygen is $\dfrac{4}{3} \times 9x = 12x$.

The mass ratio of C : H : O is $9x : x : 12x = 9 : 1 : 12$.

To find the mole ratio, we divide the mass ratio by the respective atomic masses:
Moles of C $= \dfrac{9}{12} = 0.75$
Moles of H $= \dfrac{1}{1} = 1$
Moles of O $= \dfrac{12}{16} = 0.75$

The simplest whole number ratio is obtained by dividing by $0.75$ and multiplying by $3$ (or simply multiplying the ratios by $4$):
C : H : O $= 3 : 4 : 3$

The empirical formula of the compound is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$.
Empirical formula mass $= (3 \times 12) + (4 \times 1) + (3 \times 16) = 36 + 4 + 48 = 88\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

The multiplying factor $n = \dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}} = \dfrac{176}{88} = 2$.

The molecular formula is $(\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_3)_2 = \text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6$.

Therefore, the number of hydrogen atoms present in one molecule of the compound is $8$.

Answer: $8$

questions.question:

[Given: Molar atomic mass in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $P = 31$, $O = 16$]
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation is:
$P_4(s) + 5O_2(g) \rightarrow P_4O_{10}(s)$

Molar mass of $P_4O_{10} = 4 \times 31 + 10 \times 16 = 124 + 160 = 284\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
Moles of $P_4O_{10}$ formed $= \dfrac{71.0}{284} = 0.25\text{ mol}$.

From the stoichiometry, $1\text{ mol}$ of $P_4O_{10}$ requires $5\text{ mol}$ of $O_2$ and $1\text{ mol}$ of $P_4$.
Moles of $O_2$ reacted $= 0.25 \times 5 = 1.25\text{ mol}$.
Moles of $P_4$ reacted $= 0.25 \times 1 = 0.25\text{ mol}$.

Since $O_2$ is completely consumed, the initial moles of $O_2 = 1.25\text{ mol}$.
Total initial moles in the mixture $= 3.0\text{ mol}$.
Initial moles of $P_4 = 3.0 - 1.25 = 1.75\text{ mol}$.

Moles of unreacted $P_4 = 1.75 - 0.25 = 1.50\text{ mol}$.
Mass of unreacted $P_4 = 1.50 \times 124 = 186\text{ g}$.

Answer: $186\text{ g}$
